title: Chapter VIII

teacherSummary.text: At Netherfield the Bingley sisters mock Elizabeth's muddy petticoat. Darcy, Miss Bingley and Elizabeth debate what makes an 'accomplished' woman; Darcy adds 'extensive reading.'

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter VIII,” how does Austen show the accomplished woman? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter VIII develops the idea of the accomplished woman. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and irony shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses characterization in Chapter VIII to complicate the reader's understanding of the accomplished woman. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter VIII within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of the accomplished woman responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter VIII as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of the accomplished woman. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

segments.activity: Quick-write and share on the opening question.
segments.script: Good morning, readers. Before we open the book, take three minutes and write your honest answer to this: What does the debate about accomplishments reveal about each speaker? There is no wrong answer yet; we will test our ideas against the text today.

segments.activity: Model pronouncing, defining and using five key words in context.
segments.script: Today's words include undervaluing, netting, scampering, solaced, inattention. Watch how I figure out a word from its sentence before I check the dictionary. Here is the line: ““Eliza Bennet,” said Miss Bingley, when the door was closed on her, “is one of those young ladies who seek to recommend themselves to the other sex, by undervaluing their own; and with many men, I dare say, it succeeds.” My guess comes from the clues around it; the dictionary says: To value, rate, or estimate below the real worth.

segments.activity: Present background, then the significance of the chapter.
segments.script: Let me give you some background that the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. Female 'accomplishments' (music, drawing, languages) were valued as marriage assets. Now, why does this chapter matter? Elizabeth's skepticism about impossible standards is a sly critique of how women were judged. As you listen, jot one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Characterization, Irony, Theme.
segments.script: Let's read this passage together. I will read the first sentence; you track along. Every time you spot characterization, mark it. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice here? I will collect three ideas on the board and we will choose the strongest one together, using the evidence.
